extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students (learning proof techniques; solving textbook exercises)
extracted.subtask_description: Producing rigorous written solutions to undergraduate-level textbook exercises (proofs by induction, set theory, relations, sequences, combinatorics, and basic analysis). Emphasises standard proof patterns, counterexamples, and element-wise reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard mathematical induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove a statement for all n by showing a base case holds and an inductive step: assume the statement for n = ℓ (or for all k ≤ ℓ as appropriate) and deduce it for n = ℓ + 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check and state the base case explicitly (sometimes F0, F1 or n=1). In the inductive step substitute the inductive hypothesis and perform algebraic manipulation to obtain the ℓ+1 case. Examples: Fibonacci identities, Binomial Theorem, many recurrence proofs in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an inductive hypothesis that assumes the statement for all integers ≤ k (not just k) to prove it for k+1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sufficient base cases (often multiple, e.g., n=0 and n=1 or p=8,9,10) so the inductive machinery can be applied. Used for problems like coin/price decompositions and sequences defined by recurrences that require earlier terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction with case splitting (parity/divisibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the recurrence or claim behaves differently for even/odd or divisibility classes, split the inductive step into cases and handle each separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate both cases fully (e.g., k = 2j and k = 2j+1) and show the required inequality or identity in each. Example: recurrence T(n) bounded by n log2 n + n, treated separately for even and odd n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove set equality by two inclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: To show A = B, prove A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A by element-wise reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with an arbitrary element of one side, use definitions to deduce membership on the other side. Examples: intersection of graphs F ∩ G = {(0,2),(4,6)}, power set equalities, Cartesian product intersections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproof by explicit counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a universal claim is false, provide a concrete counterexample where the claim fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose minimal/simple examples (small finite sets or small integers) to exhibit failure. Examples: false set equalities involving power sets and differences; divisibility set counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive Pascal's identity algebraically
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove (n choose r) + (n choose r−1) = (n+1 choose r) by expanding binomial coefficients via factorials and algebraic simplification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manipulate factorial expressions, align denominators and numerators, and simplify to obtain the (n+1) choose form; explicit factorial steps are shown in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binomial theorem by induction (with re-indexing and grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove (a+b)^{n} = sum_{k=0}^n (n choose k) a^{n−k} b^{k} by base case and inductive step: multiply the n-case by (a+b), re-index the summations, group similar powers, and apply Pascal's identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extract the first and last terms explicitly, re-index inner sums (replace k by k−1 where needed), group coefficients with same powers of a and b, then use Pascal to combine coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-indexing sums to align indices
rubrics_metrics.description: When working with sums in induction, replace the summation index (e.g., k→k−1) to align powers and combine terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully adjust summation limits after re-indexing and ensure no terms are lost; used in binomial theorem inductive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration by parts for Laplace transforms and higher derivatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Use integration by parts to prove ℒ{f'}(s) = sℒ{f}(s) − f(0), and then extend to ℒ{f^{(k)}} by induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify boundary terms vanish (assumptions on f so f(t)e^{−st}→0 as t→∞). For higher derivatives use the inductive formula and absorb terms into the sum of initial values, as shown in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove sequence formulas using recurrence plus induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume an explicit closed form for earlier terms and substitute into the recurrence to verify the closed form for the next term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraically manipulate the recurrence with the inductive hypothesis to match the claimed closed form (e.g., a_n = (−2)^n + 3^n). Show how terms combine to produce the next exponentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartesian product reasoning and edge cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Use element-wise definitions of A×B to prove identities like A×∅=∅ and inclusion A×C ⊆ B×C when A⊆B (with attention to C empty/non-empty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why A×∅ has no elements and handle the special case C=∅ separately; when proving strict inclusion show existence of b∈B\,A and pair (b,c) ∈ B×C but not in A×C when C≠∅.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power set cardinality by induction (|P(A)| = 2^n)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove number of subsets of an n-element set is 2^n by splitting subsets into those that contain a chosen element and those that don't.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let B˜ be A without one element; show P(A) partitions into two disjoint sets each in bijection with P(B˜), hence |P(A)| = 2|P(B˜)| and conclude by induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element-chasing for set operation proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish identities/inclusions about unions, intersections, differences by tracking arbitrary element membership conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with arbitrary element x in one side, unpack definitions (e.g., x∈A and x∈B) and derive membership on the other; used throughout set exercises (intersections, unions, complements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremum vs maximum: proofs and counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a number is the supremum, prove it's an upper bound and no smaller number is an upper bound; to show no maximum, show for any candidate element there exists a larger element in the set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit constructions (midpoint trick) to produce larger elements; note completeness of R ensures sup exists for nonempty bounded sets, while rationals lack this property (counterexample with √2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unions/intersections of sequences of sets via constructive N
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove equalities like ⋃_{n≥3} (1/n,1−1/n) = (0,1) or ⋂_{n≥1} (−1/n,1+1/n) = [0,1] by constructing appropriate N given an element and using inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given x∈(0,1), choose N large enough so 1/N < min(x,1−x) to place x in (1/N,1−1/N); conversely show any element of left side lies in right side.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone sequence convergence to supremum (ε−N proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (a_n) is nondecreasing and bounded above, then a = sup{a_n} and a_n → a; prove by ε−N argument: for given ε>0 find N with a_N > a−ε, and then for n≥N have |a_n−a|<ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use that a−ε is not an upper bound to find N. Provide explicit inequalities to bound difference by ε.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Division Algorithm and residue analysis for modular classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify integers modulo m by writing x = mq + r (0 ≤ r < m) and examine x^2 remainders to determine equivalence classes (e.g., mod 3 analysis for x^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute squares for representatives r and deduce which residues occur; used to identify equivalence classes under relation 3 | (x^2−y^2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence relation verification and finding classes
rubrics_metrics.description: To show relation R is an equivalence relation, verify reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity; then describe equivalence classes explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply definitions to generic elements and use algebraic or geometric interpretation to describe classes (e.g., circles of equal radius, lines of same slope, congruence classes mod 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial splitting/counting via casework and algebra
rubrics_metrics.description: Count outcomes by splitting into exhaustive cases and combining counts algebraically (e.g., splitting stones into piles yields (n(n−1))/2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider special-case splits (1 and n−1) separately from p,q>1, apply inductive hypothesis for subpiles, simplify algebraically to arrive at closed-form expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate failure of properties with explicit numeric counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Show a property (reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity) fails by producing concrete numbers/functions/sets where premises hold but conclusion does not (e.g., |x−y|<1 not transitive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick small rational or integer values illustrating the violation; state explicitly which property fails and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify boundary term elimination in improper integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: When integrating to infinity (e.g., in Laplace transform integration by parts), state and use assumptions that ensure boundary term f(t)e^{−st}→0 as t→∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly cite the required hypothesis (growth/decay conditions) and show the limit is zero before discarding the term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure properties for function-difference relations
rubrics_metrics.description: When relation is defined by linearity of differences (f−g linear), show reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity by algebraic closure under addition/subtraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that f−f is linear (zero), g−f is negative of f−g (hence linear), and sum of linear functions is linear, concluding equivalence.
